constraint.instructions: Read `frame`. Does {item} violate a HARD constraint stated in `frame` — the time window, the team size, a required technology, the budget, or a stated invariant? Judge only against constraints the frame states explicitly. A constraint that is merely difficult is not violated; a constraint that cannot be met as written is.

criteria.true: It violates at least one hard constraint stated in `frame`.
criteria.false: It respects every hard constraint stated in `frame`.

anti_goal.instructions: Read `anti_goals`. Is {item} PRIMARILY one of the listed anti-goals? Judge the centre of the idea, not an incidental feature: an idea that happens to contain a listed pattern as one small part is not primarily that pattern.

criteria.true: Its core mechanism is one of the listed anti-goals.
criteria.false: Its core mechanism is something other than the listed anti-goals.

demo.instructions: Read the time window in `frame`. Would {item} FAIL to produce a working, demonstrable result inside that window — something a person could run end to end and watch work, not a design document or a partial component? If `frame` states no time window, answer false.

criteria.true: No working, demonstrable result is reachable within the stated window.
criteria.false: A working, demonstrable result is reachable within the stated window, or no window is stated.

checkpoint.instructions: Read the time window in `frame`. Would {item} FAIL to reach a first decision checkpoint inside that window — a point producing evidence that it works or that it should stop? If `frame` states no time window, answer false.

criteria.true: No decision checkpoint producing real evidence is reachable within the stated window.
criteria.false: A decision checkpoint producing real evidence is reachable within the stated window, or no window is stated.

access.instructions: Does {item} depend on data, system access, partnerships or permissions that the team described in `frame` cannot realistically obtain? Judge obtainability for THIS team, not in principle.

criteria.true: It depends on data, access or partners the team cannot realistically obtain.
criteria.false: Everything it depends on is obtainable by this team.

triage.instructions: How promising is {item} as an answer to `frame`, weighing depth, robustness and feasibility together, as judged by {evaluator}?
criteria: Not worth pursuing: it does not answer the frame, or it is a restatement of the problem.
Weak: it answers the frame only partially, or its mechanism is unlikely to hold up.
Plausible: it answers the frame and the mechanism is credible, but nothing about it stands out.
Strong: it answers the frame well, the mechanism is sound, and at least one aspect is notably good.
Outstanding: it answers the frame convincingly, the mechanism is sound and well chosen, and it would be hard to improve on within the constraints.

agentic-software.evaluator: a senior engineering director evaluating a GitHub submission

signal.instructions: Judge the engineering depth of {item}: does it carry explicit state, real orchestration across steps, and verification of its own output — or is it a single model call wearing an interface?
criteria: Fluff: an LLM call with a UI around it.
Thin: one loop, no verification of the output.
Moderate: a stateful loop, but verification is weak or implicit.
Strong: stateful, verified, and able to correct itself on failure.
Exceptional: a deterministic envelope around non-deterministic agents, verified at every step.

resilience.instructions: Judge how {item} behaves under hostile reality: unstructured input, malformed or failing API responses, timeouts, and prompt injection carried in data it processes.
criteria: Assumes the happy path throughout.
Handles errors only where they are convenient to handle.
Handles common failures, but untrusted input is still treated as trusted.
Handles failure and timeout paths, and separates untrusted data from instructions.
Degrades safely under every named failure, with an explicit trust boundary and a bounded blast radius.

buildability.instructions: Judge whether the team in `frame` could actually build {item} to a demonstrable state inside the stated constraints.
criteria: Not buildable by this team in this window.
Buildable only by cutting the parts that make it interesting.
Buildable, but the window leaves no room for anything going wrong.
Comfortably buildable with slack for iteration.
Buildable quickly, leaving most of the window for depth.

pain.instructions: How acute is the problem {item} addresses for the user named in it — is this something they already spend money, time or worry on?
criteria: No evident pain: a solution looking for a problem.
Mild annoyance: real but tolerated indefinitely.
Recognised problem: people complain, few act.
Acute: people already spend money or meaningful time on workarounds.
Urgent: it blocks something the user must do, and they are actively shopping for a fix.

differentiation.instructions: How hard would it be for an existing incumbent or a fast follower to copy {item} once it is visible?
criteria: Trivially copied; no distinct insight.
Mostly a feature an incumbent would ship in a quarter.
Some distinct insight, but no durable barrier.
A real insight others have not acted on, with some accumulating advantage.
A structural advantage that strengthens with use and is costly to replicate.

reachability.instructions: How plausibly can the team reach its first ten real users for {item} without a budget or an existing audience?
criteria: No identifiable channel to the first user.
A channel exists but requires budget or introductions the team lacks.
Reachable with effort through general channels.
A specific, named channel where these users already gather.
The team can reach the first ten users this week through existing relationships.

validation.instructions: How cheaply and quickly could the riskiest assumption behind {item} be tested before building it?
criteria: The only test is building the whole thing.
Testing requires most of the build.
Testable with a substantial prototype.
Testable in days with a thin artefact.
Testable this week with conversations or a landing page, before any code.

architecture.evaluator: a principal engineer in a design review

simplicity.instructions: Judge the number of moving parts {item} introduces, and how much a new engineer must hold in their head to change it safely.
criteria: Very complex: many new components and non-obvious interactions.
Complex: several new components, with coupling that is hard to reason about.
Moderate: a manageable number of parts with clear responsibilities.
Simple: few parts, each with one job, composed in an obvious way.
Trivially simple: it removes moving parts rather than adding them.

isolation.instructions: If one component of {item} fails or degrades, how far does the damage spread?
criteria: Any single failure takes the whole system down.
Failures spread across unrelated features.
Failures are contained to a subsystem, but recovery is manual.
Failures are contained and the system degrades gracefully.
Failures are contained, self-healing, and invisible to the user path that does not depend on them.

load.instructions: How does {item} behave at ten times the load described in `frame`?
criteria: Breaks well before 10x and the fix is a redesign.
Needs significant rework to reach 10x.
Reaches 10x with tuning and more hardware.
Reaches 10x by scaling out, with a known bottleneck that is addressable.
Reaches 10x with no structural change; the scaling path is explicit.

reversibility.instructions: If {item} turns out to be the wrong choice in six months, how costly is it to back out?
criteria: Effectively permanent; backing out means a rewrite.
Expensive to reverse; data and contracts would have to migrate.
Reversible with a planned migration.
Reversible behind an interface, with limited blast radius.
Trivially reversible: it can be switched off without touching callers.

upside.instructions: If {item} works as intended, how materially does it change the position of the organisation described in `frame`?
criteria: Negligible even if it fully succeeds.
A marginal improvement to an existing line.
A meaningful improvement to an existing line.
Opens a new line or materially changes the cost base.
Changes what the organisation is, not only what it earns.

defensibility.instructions: If {item} succeeds visibly, what stops a better-resourced competitor from taking the position?
criteria: Nothing: success invites immediate replication.
A short head start only.
Some switching cost or know-how, but no durable moat.
A real barrier: data, relationships, regulation or scale economics.
A compounding barrier that widens with every customer.

execution.instructions: Can the organisation described in `frame` actually execute {item} with the people and capabilities it has or can hire?
criteria: Requires capabilities the organisation has no path to.
Requires substantial hiring or acquisition before starting.
Executable, but it stretches the current team.
Within current capability with focused effort.
Plays directly to capabilities the organisation already has.

reversibility.instructions: If {item} proves wrong, how much is lost and how easily can the organisation step back?
criteria: A one-way door: failure is existential or unwindable.
Costly to unwind, with lasting commitments.
Unwindable with a real write-off.
Unwindable with limited loss; commitments are staged.
Cheap to stop at any point; each stage is independently valuable.
